A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same human–LLM politeness study. The main text, five figures, tables, and Appendices A–C are readable and can be matched across revisions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM experiments, human response collection and preference evaluations, and linguistic analyses. These extend beyond the human results attributed to Yoon et al. (2020).

after.justification: v2 retains those original empirical results and additionally reports smaller-model calibration, US–UK subgroup findings, and annotation-agreement results.

M1.justification: The prompting procedures, generation approach, politeness taxonomy, and LLM-assisted annotation with manual correction are retained. Appendix C.5 expands documentation of correction practices without establishing a change to the underlying method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same English-language scenarios, constrained and open-ended tasks, and US/UK participant populations. The new country comparison reanalyzes existing participants, and the smaller-model calibration uses the existing 208 scenarios.

E2.justification: Appendix B.6 adds an open-ended comparison of an 8B model with the larger models; v1 evaluated the 8B models only in the constrained experiment. B.6 introduces it as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct but subsequently calls it Llama-3.1-8B. The main human preference comparison retains GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct.

E3.justification: The added calibration collects 208 smaller-model responses and truncates them to the first complete sentence before strategy annotation and comparison (Appendix B.6). Appendix C.5 adds exact-set agreement as an annotation-evaluation metric. The original generation settings and human evaluation design are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds an exploratory US–UK strategy comparison, smaller-model failure examples and distribution comparisons, and a more detailed annotation-error analysis (Section 5.3; Appendices B.6 and C.5). These are bounded additions to the existing goal/rating, negation, lexical, and embedding analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix C.5 adds annotation-reliability reporting through strict exact-set agreement between the two LLM annotators and against human-corrected labels; v1 reported distributional JSD comparisons. The existing confidence-interval practices, main significance tests, and generation repetition counts remain unchanged.

E6.justification: The main numerical results remain unchanged, including Table 1 and the 66% preference for LLM responses. New results include US–UK JSD = 0.5279, smaller-model versus larger-model JSD values exceeding 0.53, and p < 0.001 for those comparisons. Appendix C.5 reports 39.8% inter-annotator agreement and agreement with corrected labels of 36.1% for GPT-4.1 and 34.3% for Claude-3.7-Sonnet.

T1.justification: Neither version develops new mathematical propositions or proofs. The added relational-work and Gricean discussion is conceptual interpretation, and the exact-match agreement criterion is an empirical evaluation metric.

C1.justification: The three principal contributions and headline empirical claims are retained. The abstract and introduction explicitly restrict the study to English-language scenarios, while the discussion reframes its contribution as descriptive evidence for intentional AI communication design rather than prescribing human-like politeness.

C2.justification: v1 characterizes the strategy divergence as fundamental misalignment. v2 develops an alternative relational explanation and recognizes that maintaining distance may suit expectations for AI systems. It also adds substantive qualifications concerning English-only coverage, persona-induced stereotypes, third-person evaluations, and the imbalanced US–UK analysis.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1.1 and Table 9 newly disclose participant demographics. Appendix C.5 documents how the authors established correction criteria and independently reviewed annotations, with concrete correction examples. These expand reproducibility information; the existing prompts and code/data access statement are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature on relational politeness and rapport management, including Spencer-Oatey, Locher, and Watts, alongside work on listener adaptation, cultural variation, and implicit personalization. This broadens the discussion's research context while retaining the original related-work organization and empirical contribution positioning.

P1.justification: The former Conclusion is extensively rewritten as Discussion, with coordinated revisions to the abstract, introduction, and Limitations. New appendix subsections organize demographic, calibration, and annotation-correction material. The revision also introduces editorial defects, including duplicated annotation prose in Section 5.3 and an unresolved figure cross-reference in Appendix B.2.

P2.justification: v2 adds a compact main-text strategy-example table drawing on the existing appendix material (Table 2) and a participant-demographics table (Table 9), and revises Table 1's caption. All five figures are retained unchanged; existing tables are renumbered and surrounding content reflows.

improvement.justification: v2 improves transparency about annotation quality and participant composition, and gives the retained findings a more qualified, explicitly descriptive interpretation. These are useful but limited gains. The additions also contain an unresolved reporting inconsistency: Section 5.3's 532 US versus 92 UK responses do not reconcile with Table 9's 80.1% versus 19.9% participant split under the stated four-responses-per-person design. New duplicated prose and a broken cross-reference further temper the improvement.
